name: heed (LMDB bindings)
baseline: RocksDB (rust-rocksdb 0.22) and SQLite (rusqlite 0.37, bundled, default rollback journal) as key-value stores
verdict_reason: LMDB through heed had the fastest reads in redb's comparison, 4.6x faster than RocksDB and 6.7x faster than SQLite single-threaded, and the fastest bulk load. It was 2.1x slower than RocksDB on batch writes and 1.5x slower on removals, and used 3x the disk.
tier_reason: Third-party benchmark (redb's author) with public source, pinned toolchain, and stated CPU and SSD.
claimed_speedup: Random reads 637 vs 2911 ms for RocksDB (4.6x) and 4283 ms for SQLite (6.7x); 32-thread reads 125 vs 1100 ms (8.8x) and 26536 ms; bulk load 9232 vs 13969 ms (1.5x). Slower: batch writes 942 vs 451 ms, removals 10435 vs 6900 ms; uncompacted size 2.61 GiB vs 893.18 MiB (ratios derived from page data).
workload: 5 million random 24-byte keys with 150-byte values: bulk load, 1,000 durable single-insert transactions, 100 batches of 1,000, 1 million random reads (1 to 32 threads), removals.
toolchain: rustc 1.89, heed 0.22, cargo bench release profile
platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, BSDs; needs mmap
one_liner: Typed Rust wrapper over LMDB; fastest reads in redb's comparison, 4.6x RocksDB, but slower batch writes and 3x the disk.
how_it_is_fast: LMDB memory-maps the whole database and serves reads straight from the OS page cache with no user-space cache or copy. Its copy-on-write B+tree lets readers proceed lock-free alongside one writer, which is why read throughput scales with threads.
use_it_when: Read-dominated workloads, especially many concurrent readers
Bulk loading a dataset that is then mostly read
skip_it_when: Write-heavy or delete-heavy workloads, where RocksDB and fjall were faster
Disk space is tight: LMDB used about 3x RocksDB's space
You need the data set to exceed the configured map size without planning for it
caveats: Measured by redb's author in August 2025 with heed 0.22; heed is now 0.23
LMDB has no user-space cache, so the 4 GB cache given to the other engines did not apply to it; it relies on the OS page cache
tradeoffs: Opening an environment is unsafe in heed because the memory map must not be changed by other code
Fixed maximum map size; one writer at a time
C library underneath; no checksums on pages read from disk

evidence.quote: | uncompacted size | 4.00 GiB | 2.61 GiB | **893.18 MiB** | 1000.95 MiB | 1.09 GiB |
Results collected on a Ryzen 9950X3D with Samsung 9100 PRO NVMe.
LMDB and SQLite do not perform checksum checks when retrieving pages from disk
